newsitem.title: USA: Perry undecided on whether to leave Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: Perry undecided on whether to leave Pentagon.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Perry said on Friday he will decide after next month's U.S. presidential election whether to resign or to remain at the Pentagon if he is asked to stay by the winner.

"This is a big personal decision for me to make. I will not make it in a theoretical sense. I will make it only if and when I am confronted with the alternative," he told reporters in response to questions aboard his aircraft as he flew home from a three-day visit to Russia.

"I don't think there is any good time or bad time walking away from the job as secretary of defence," added Perry, who turned 69 on Oct. 11. "There is always a problem. There is always a crisis. There's always some programme that is halfway completed."

President Bill Clinton leads Republican challenger Bob Dole by a wide margin in national polls, but if Dole wins he would be expected to follow precedent and reach into Republican ranks for a new secretary of defence.
Perry, who took the job in 1994 after Les Aspin resigned under pressure, said in an interview published in the Wall Street Journal last week that he had not made up his mind.
"I should, for point of reference, say that I had not decided to take this job in the first place. It was not something I sought, something I was anxious to do," said Perry.
"It was something which was urged on me and after a lot of consideration I finally decided to do."

Despite problems over continued U.S. peacekeeping in Bosnia and questions about responsibility for two bomb blasts in Saudi Arabia that killed more than 20 U.S. troops, Perry is considered by many experts to be one of the strongest and most popular defence secretaries in decades.
But he has also undertaken a crushing work and travel schedule that would leave many less active persons exhausted.

Previously published reports have said that Secretary of State Warren Christopher intends to leave his job whether or not President Clinton is re-elected and that Perry wants to return some day to private life and perhaps teaching.

"When I am confronted with the decision to make, I will make it. I am known as a decisive manager and I will make it and make it very promptly," said Perry. " It is just too hard to concentrate on it as a hypothetical situation."

Perry, in response to questions, expressed some pride in Pentagon initiatives under him to sharply cut Cold War nuclear weapons in the United States and former Soviet Union, to improve support for military personnel and dependents and reform the way the Pentagon buys arms and equipment to save billions of dollars.

"Whenever I leave the defence department, I would like to be able to look back and say first of all (that) I have done something significant and, secondly, many of the long-term programmes that I have worked on will continue long after I leave," he said.
